intro: This guide takes your group through A Retrospect (For Teens) in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It retells Hudson Taylor’s own account of how a doubting teenager came to faith, learned to trust God with money and danger, went to China and founded the China Inland Mission. It is written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group, and it is especially good for young people who have honest doubts or wonder whether prayer really works.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying, in your own words or inviting a volunteer to pray, about what the chapter raised (2–3 minutes). Each chapter ends with a “One thing to do” challenge, which is worth reading out before people leave.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and glance at the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens. The book includes a poor family with a dying mother, Taylor’s own brush with a deadly infection, a storm at sea, a robbery and real hunger, and it speaks often about praying for family members who do not believe. Some in your group may be praying for someone who has not come to faith, or may have watched a prayer go unanswered, so honour the book’s own care not to treat prayer or giving as a formula. Be gentle with anyone who has known serious illness or loss, keep personal reflection private, and be ready to talk one-to-one afterwards.

weeks.summary: Hudson Taylor grew up in a Christian home but was left cold, failed to make himself a Christian by effort, and took up sceptical views, though he vowed that if he ever believed the Bible he would really put it to the test. At about fifteen, bored at home, he picked up a Gospel booklet and was caught by the phrase “the finished work of Christ.” Realising the debt was already paid, he knelt and accepted it. The big idea: salvation is received as a finished gift, not earned, and honest doubts do not shut God out.

memory_verse.text: When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, ‘It is finished,’ and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

activity.title: Gift or Wage?
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: Write two headings: “A wage” and “A gift.”
As a group, list the differences: how each is received, who gets the credit, whether it can be lost.
Discuss: which way do most people think about being right with God, and why?
Read the memory verse and ask what the word “finished” rules out.
Invite everyone to spend a minute privately telling God honestly where they stand.

weeks.summary: On the afternoon Hudson read the booklet, his mother, many miles away, locked herself in her room to pray for him until she was moved to thank God that it was done. When he came home a fortnight later she already knew, and he later found in his sister Amelia’s diary a resolve to pray for him daily, written a month before his conversion. The book warns that prayer is not a machine, but shows two people who kept praying for one person without any visible sign. The big idea: keep praying for others and do not lose heart.

memory_verse.text: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.

activity.title: A Name to Pray For
steps: Discuss the chapter’s warning: why is it wrong to treat prayer as a machine?
Ask: what is the difference between quitting prayer and quietly drifting from it?
Give each person a card to write, privately, the name of one person they long to see come to God.
Ask everyone to decide how long they will pray for that person daily, and write it on the card.
Encourage them to keep the card somewhere they will see it.

weeks.summary: Training as a doctor in Hull, Taylor was teaching himself to depend on God alone and had just one half-crown left when a poor man asked him to pray for his dying wife. In a starving family’s room, he felt a hypocrite for urging them to trust a Father he would not trust beyond his coin; he admitted he could trust “God plus one-and-sixpence” but not God only. He gave the coin, walked home singing, and the next morning received half a sovereign, though the book warns this is not a formula. The big idea: trusting God with a safety margin is not yet trusting him fully.

memory_verse.text: Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.

activity.title: Finding the Line
steps: Explain Taylor’s phrase “God plus one-and-sixpence” and what it meant.
Discuss the chapter’s warning against treating God like an investment app.
As a group, list things besides money where people keep a safety margin with God, such as time, reputation or control.
Ask each person to write privately where their own “one-and-sixpence” line might be.
Challenge everyone to think of one wise, not reckless, way to step past it this week.

weeks.summary: Taylor decided not to remind his busy employer that his salary was due, but to ask God to bring it to the doctor’s mind, to learn to move people through God by prayer alone. When the doctor finally remembered, he had just sent all his money to the bank; but late that night a wealthy patient arrived to pay his bill in cash, and the doctor handed Taylor the notes. God answered, but not in the way Taylor expected. The big idea: God promises to supply our needs, but not always through the door we are staring at.

memory_verse.text: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: The Script and the Answer
steps: Retell the two halves of Taylor’s Saturday: the reminder and the money came from different people.
Ask each person to think privately of something they are praying about.
Have them write down, for themselves, the exact outcome they have quietly decided would count as an answer.
Underneath, have them list two or three other ways God could meet the same need.
Discuss as a group: why do we tend to script God’s answers?

weeks.summary: In London, living on bread, water and apples, Taylor pricked his finger with a needle and the next day dissected the body of someone who had died of a dangerous fever. He fell gravely ill and a surgeon told him, “You are a dead man,” yet Taylor felt sure he still had work to do in China. He lanced the wound, accepted treatment his uncle paid for, and survived, while two others wounded at the same time died. The big idea: a settled sense that our life belongs to God keeps us calm without making us careless.

memory_verse.text: I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD.

activity.title: Two Questions
steps: Write two questions where everyone can see them: “Is this dangerous?” and “Is this the end of me?”
In small groups, list setbacks teenagers face that can feel like “you are finished,” such as a failed exam or a rejection.
For each, talk through how to take the danger seriously without handing over the verdict on your future.
Discuss how Taylor held both: he used medical treatment and still trusted God’s purpose.

weeks.summary: In September 1853 Taylor sailed for China on the Dumfries, and his mother’s cry of anguish at the parting taught him what “God so loved the world” costs. A gale drove the ship to within a stone’s throw of the rocks of Carnarvon Bay before the wind shifted and they escaped. Taylor had thrown away his swimming-belt that night, thinking he could not trust God while owning it, but later decided this was a mistake: faith does not mean refusing the means God provides. The big idea: trusting God and using the help he gives are never enemies.

memory_verse.text: He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.

activity.title: Faith or Superstition?
steps: Read out short situations, such as “I’m trusting God, so I won’t revise for the test,” or “I’ll pray about my injury and also see a doctor.”
After each one, the group votes by standing up for “real faith” or staying seated for “superstition dressed as faith.”
Discuss any situation where opinions split.
Ask: what was Taylor’s swimming-belt mistake, and how did he correct it?
Challenge everyone to pray and act on one thing this week.

weeks.summary: Near New Guinea the wind died and a current dragged the Dumfries toward hidden reefs, with people gathering on the shore. When the captain said everything had been done, Taylor proposed that the four Christians on board agree together in prayer for a breeze; while praying he felt sure it was granted, and he told the sneering first officer to let down the mainsail. The top sail began to tremble, the wind came, and the ship escaped. The big idea: specific prayer, prayed together, lets us see God’s faithfulness clearly.

memory_verse.text: Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven.

activity.title: From Vague to Specific
steps: As a group, list some common vague prayers, such as “bless everyone” or “help me with school.”
Discuss why vague prayers feel safe and what they can never teach us.
In pairs, rewrite each vague prayer as a specific one, without sharing anything private.
Invite anyone who wants to pair up with a friend to agree in prayer about one specific thing this week.

weeks.summary: In China, Taylor at first kept his English clothes and was shouted at as a foreigner wherever he went. He adopted Chinese dress and hairstyle, which felt like a loss of status, and found quiet listeners and open homes, while his friend William Burns, still in English clothes, drew crowds of gawkers until he humbled himself and changed too. Taylor laid down his image so that nothing about him would get in the way of the message. The big idea: love is willing to give up status and image so others can hear about Jesus.

memory_verse.text: To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.

activity.title: What Gets in the Way?
steps: Discuss what Taylor gave up when he changed his dress, and why it was mainly pride rather than comfort.
In small groups, list things about Christians today that might put up barriers for people before they hear a word.
Then list ways to close distance with people who are different or left out, such as at school.
Point out that Taylor’s convictions never changed, only his image, and discuss the difference.
Ask each person to think privately of one person they could move toward this week.

weeks.summary: On the way to Ningpo, Taylor’s hired servant disappeared with nearly everything he owned. Turned away from inns in Hai-ning, he slept on temple steps with his money under his head, and kept would-be thieves away all night by singing hymns, reciting Scripture and praying aloud. Afterwards he was ashamed that he had been more troubled about his luggage than about the people around him who did not know Christ, and he thought of Jesus, who had nowhere to lay his head. The big idea: losing things hurts, but it should help us get our priorities in proportion.

memory_verse.text: And Jesus said to him, ‘Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’

activity.title: Getting the Proportions Right
steps: Ask each person to write privately a list of losses that would make them panic most, such as a phone, a friendship or a plan.
Have them rate each from 1 to 10 for how much panic it would cause.
Then ask: how much do I feel about where people around me stand with God?
Discuss as a group, without anyone needing to share their list, what Taylor noticed about his own heart.

weeks.summary: The servant had deliberately stolen about forty pounds’ worth of goods, and Taylor could have had him punished. Instead, because he had been praying for the man and reading the Sermon on the Mount with him, he wrote him a letter pleading with him to repent and trust Christ. The book is honest that there is no record of a reply, but a friend in England, moved by the story, sent Taylor forty pounds and became a regular supporter. The big idea: when someone wrongs us, we can refuse to let their evil make us hard and answer it with good.

memory_verse.text: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

activity.title: Overcoming with Good
steps: Discuss why the culture says “make them pay” and what Taylor chose instead.
Talk about the difference between forgiving someone and pretending the wrong did not happen.
In small groups, brainstorm concrete good things a person could do toward someone who has wronged them, such as praying for them or speaking fairly about them.
Ask each person to think privately of one person and choose one good thing to do this week.

weeks.summary: In Ningpo, Taylor resigned from a society that had fallen into debt, determined to owe no one anything, while he and Mr. Jones fed many poor people each day. On 6 January 1858 they were down to a single cash, the floating bridge they needed to cross to sell their stove had been swept away, and the ferry cost two cash each. They drank cocoa, knelt to pray for daily bread, and while they were still on their knees a letter arrived with money from England. The big idea: God does not always spare us the bottom, but he is trustworthy within it.

memory_verse.text: The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.

activity.title: Ebenezer and Jehovah-Jireh
steps: Explain the two scrolls over Taylor’s mantelpiece: “Hitherto the Lord has helped us” and “The Lord will provide.”
Ask each person to write privately one time God has helped them so far.
Then have them write one present need they are bringing to God.
Discuss the chapter’s caution: why should we not turn this story into a promise of last-minute cash?

weeks.summary: Failing health sent Taylor back to England, where a map of China showed him eleven inland provinces with no missionary. He was sure God would supply workers but refused for a long time to ask, afraid of being blamed if young workers suffered, until on 25 June 1865 he walked out of a church in Brighton onto the beach and handed all the responsibility to God. He asked for twenty-four workers and wrote the request in the margin of his Bible, and that prayer became the China Inland Mission, with a party sailing on the Lammermuir in May 1866. The big idea: our part is to obey; the results belong to God.

memory_verse.text: Then he said to his disciples, ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.’

activity.title: Written in the Margin
steps: Discuss what actually held Taylor back: fear of being blamed, not doubt that God could act.
Ask each person to think of a step they have been avoiding because of how it might reflect on them.
Have them write it down privately as a specific request or plan, with a date.
Underneath, have them write: “The obeying is mine, the results are yours.”
Look back over the whole book together and name the lesson about trust that stood out most.
